injection-attacks.title: Welcome to Injection: SQL and command, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
injection-attacks.idea: Injection is a vulnerability where untrusted input changes the structure of a command instead of just supplying a value inside it. The program meant to ask "find the user named X"; the attacker makes it ask "find the user named X, or everyone". It appears wherever a program assembles a command from text: SQL queries, shell commands, LDAP filters, even HTML (which is why cross-site scripting is a cousin). The fix is always the same shape: keep code and data separate by using an API that accepts them as separate arguments. Parameterised queries for SQL, argument arrays for processes.
injection-attacks.example: The login below builds its query with string concatenation. Trace what happens when the attacker types ' OR '1'='1 as the username and anything as the password. 1. The developer intended: SELECT FROM users WHERE name = 'ama' AND password = 'secret'. 2. With the payload, the query becomes: SELECT FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1' AND password = 'x'. 3. '1'='1' is always true, so the WHERE matches rows regardless of the password. The first user in the table is returned, and that is usually the administrator. A comment sequence makes it cleaner: username admin'-- turns the rest of the line into a comment, so the password check disappears entirely. The fixed version passes the values separately; the database never parses them as SQL.
injection-attacks.challenge: Install OWASP Juice Shop locally (one Docker command). Find the login SQL injection, log in as admin, then open the source and write the parameterised query that would have stopped you.

xss-csrf-and-browser-defences.title: Welcome to XSS, CSRF and the browser's defences, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
xss-csrf-and-browser-defences.idea: XSS is injection into HTML. If a page prints user input without encoding it, the input can contain <script> and the browser will run it as the site: reading cookies, making requests with the victim's session, rewriting the page to capture a password. Three flavours: - Stored: the payload is saved (a comment, a profile name) and runs for everyone who views it. - Reflected: the payload is in a URL and runs when the victim clicks a crafted link. - DOM-based: client-side JavaScript itself writes untrusted data into the page with innerHTML. The defence is contextual output encoding: turn < into < when writing into HTML, and use the right encoding for attributes, URLs and JavaScript. Modern frameworks (React, Vue, templating engines) do this by default — the danger is the escape hatch (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, innerHTML).

xss-csrf-and-browser-defences.challenge: In Juice Shop, find a stored XSS and a reflected XSS. Then add a Content-Security-Policy header (via a reverse proxy or browser extension) and show that the same payload no longer executes.

authentication-and-access-control.title: Welcome to Authentication, sessions and access control, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
authentication-and-access-control.idea: Never store a password. Store a slow, salted hash of it: bcrypt, scrypt or argon2id. Slow matters: an attacker with a leaked database tries billions of guesses per second against a fast hash like MD5 or SHA-256, and thousands per second against bcrypt. The salt is a random value stored alongside the hash so that two users with the same password have different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. Also: enforce a minimum length (12+), check new passwords against known-breached lists, rate-limit login attempts per account and per IP, and never say which of username or password was wrong.

authentication-and-access-control.challenge: Pick any app you have built or have permission to test. For every endpoint, make a table: who should be allowed, then try it as a different user, as a logged-out user, and with another user's ID. Fix every row that fails.

rules-of-engagement-and-recon.title: Welcome to Rules of engagement and reconnaissance, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
rules-of-engagement-and-recon.idea: Ethical hacking is the discipline of finding weaknesses before someone with worse intentions does, and reporting them so they can be fixed. Its practitioners are judged less by the cleverness of an exploit than by the quality of their scope, their notes and their report. A finding that cannot be reproduced, or that was obtained by testing systems the client never agreed to, is worthless or harmful, however serious it looks. The lesson is built around one principle: everything you do should be explainable to the client and to a court. Each phase in this module begins with what you are permitted to do and ends with a record of what you did.

rules-of-engagement-and-recon.challenge: For a domain you own, produce a complete passive attack-surface map with sources, dates and confidence levels, and a rules-of-engagement document that would have authorised the next phase. Then write the three defensive actions you would recommend to the owner, ranked by risk and effort.

exploitation-and-privilege-escalation.title: Welcome to Exploitation and privilege escalation, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
exploitation-and-privilege-escalation.idea: A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifier names one specific publicly known flaw, for example CVE-2021-44228, the Log4Shell vulnerability in a widely used Java logging library. CVE records are maintained by a network of numbering authorities and published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) with detail and scoring. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) gives a severity score from 0.0 to 10.0 based on attributes such as whether the attack is remote, whether it needs authentication, and how much an attacker gains. A score is a starting point for prioritisation, not a verdict. A 9.8 on a service that is not reachable from the internet may matter less today than a 6.5 on the login page. The question a tester answers is whether the weakness is real in this environment, which requires confirmation. To match a version to weaknesses, search the CVE database for the product and version, then check exploit databases. searchsploit (from Exploit-DB) searches a local copy of that database and is standard on penetration testing distributions.

exploitation-and-privilege-escalation.challenge: On a TryHackMe or Hack The Box starting machine (or your own lab), document one complete path from enumeration to a proven privilege escalation. Produce a finding in the five-part format, a verified remediation, and a list of the log entries your activity created. Present the finding as if to a non-technical manager in one page.

logging-detection-and-siem.title: Welcome to Logging, detection and the SIEM, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
logging-detection-and-siem.idea: Detection is a probability problem. Every system produces far more events than anyone can read, most of them harmless, and a few that matter are hidden among them. The defender's job is to choose what to record, to make the important events easy to find, and to write rules that are specific enough to fire rarely and sensitive enough to fire when it counts. The unit of analysis throughout this lesson is the event: a timestamped record that something happened on a system, such as a login, a process start, a connection, a configuration change or a file modification. Everything else is a way of collecting, storing, correlating and deciding about events.
logging-detection-and-siem.example: Audit rules that create searchable evidence: The worked example shows the idea in code.
logging-detection-and-siem.challenge: Build a detection set for the three attacks from the offensive module: a brute-force attempt, a privilege change, and a port scan. For each, write the Sigma rule, the lab command that triggers it, the log evidence it produces, and the false positives you expect. Demonstrate that each rule fires on your attack and stays quiet during an ordinary administrator session.

hardening-patching-and-incident-response.title: Welcome to Hardening, patching and incident response, part of Cyber Security: Offense and Defense.
hardening-patching-and-incident-response.idea: Most successful intrusions use known weaknesses in systems that were not updated, accounts that should have been disabled, or services that should not have been exposed. Hardening and patching are therefore the cheapest security work available, and also the least glamorous. Incident response is the expensive counterpart: when prevention has failed, the quality of the first few hours decides whether the organisation contains the damage, preserves the evidence it needs, and recovers. Both topics come down to deciding what to do first. This lesson gives a method for those decisions.

hardening-patching-and-incident-response.challenge: Run a tabletop exercise with a partner. One person plays the attacker and makes a series of moves against the lab server; the other runs the playbook you wrote, recording timestamps in UTC. Afterwards, produce the timeline, the evidence manifest, the restore verification and a blameless review with three actions. Judge your own response against the four NIST phases.
